flutamide.summary: A prostate-cancer antiandrogen that some people use off-label to slow androgen-driven hair thinning and keep more scalp hair; liver toxicity is its main limit.

quick.overview:
Flutamide is a prescription antiandrogen approved for prostate cancer. People interested in hair use it off-label to hold on to more scalp hair, and doctors have also used it in women for excess hair growth, acne and thinning.

It blocks the androgen receptor, so testosterone and DHT have less effect on follicles and oil glands, which means slower thinning and fuller-looking hair. Its use for hair has been studied mainly in women; a French review placed it as third-line therapy for severe hirsutism, and forum comparisons with other antiandrogens are anecdotal.
quick.how: Off-label use is prescribed by a doctor, mostly for women with androgen-related hair loss, hirsutism or acne, and some online communities discuss topical or oral forms. It is usually considered after other antiandrogens, and results build over months of consistent use alongside liver monitoring.
quick.risks: The label carries a boxed warning for severe, sometimes fatal liver injury, and it is labelled for men only. Other listed effects include fetal toxicity, methemoglobinemia, hot flashes and sexual side effects in men. It is prescription-only, and guidelines rank it behind other antiandrogens because of the liver risk.

angle.text: Flutamide blocks the androgen receptor, so follicles respond less to testosterone and DHT, which means slower thinning and fuller hair. Hair-loss communities discuss topical and oral use, and clinical use for hair has been in women with androgen-related thinning.

bicalutamide.summary: A prostate-cancer antiandrogen used off-label to slow female pattern hair loss and reduce androgen effects on hair follicles; carries a liver-injury warning.

quick.overview:
Bicalutamide is a prescription antiandrogen for prostate cancer. Dermatologists sometimes prescribe it off-label for female pattern hair loss and excess hair, aiming for slower thinning and fuller-looking hair.

It binds the androgen receptor and blocks testosterone and DHT from activating it, which reduces their effect on hair follicles. The evidence for hair is reviews and retrospective data in women rather than randomised trials; a 2025 review notes off-label use to improve Sinclair grading. Some forum users also mention it for recovery after finasteride or isotretinoin, based on anecdote.
quick.how: It is taken as a prescription tablet, typically as a low-dose off-label option in women with pattern hair loss or hirsutism, often alongside other treatments. Regular liver testing is part of monitoring, and hair changes are judged over many months.
quick.risks: The label warns of severe and fatal liver injury and calls for liver testing. Hot flashes and fatigue are common in cancer patients, and off-label users report liver enzyme elevation. It is prescription-only, and hair use is off-label.

angle.text: Bicalutamide blocks the androgen receptor so follicles respond less to testosterone and DHT, slowing thinning and keeping hair fuller. It is used off-label in women with pattern hair loss, backed by retrospective data; recovery after finasteride or isotretinoin is a forum idea.

cyproterone-acetate.summary: A progestin-antiandrogen prescribed to women for hirsutism, severe acne and androgen-related hair loss; meningioma and liver risks limit long-term use.

quick.overview:
Cyproterone acetate is a prescription hormone drug that blocks androgens. Doctors use it, often with an estrogen pill, in women for excess hair growth, severe acne and androgen-related hair loss, giving calmer follicles and oil glands, clearer skin and less thinning.

It blocks androgen receptors and, as a progestin, lowers the brain signals that drive testosterone production in men and estradiol in women. A Dutch review described spironolactone or cyproterone acetate with an oral contraceptive as the safest and most effective approach for hirsutism in women with PCOS or idiopathic hirsutism. Use for appearance in men is mostly anecdotal and rarely discussed in forums.
quick.how: It is prescribed by a doctor, most often combined with an estrogen-containing pill for women with hyperandrogenism. Hair and skin changes build over months, and treatment is reviewed periodically.
quick.risks: Reported risks include meningioma at higher cumulative doses, liver toxicity, and clotting risk when combined with estrogen pills. Regulators restrict long-term high-dose use in many regions. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Cyproterone acetate blocks androgens and lowers hormone production, calming follicles and oil glands for less thinning, hirsutism and acne. It is established clinical practice for women with hyperandrogenism; appearance use in men is mostly anecdotal.

latanoprost.summary: A glaucoma eye drop whose labelled side effects include longer, thicker, darker lashes and darker irises, which is why it comes up for lashes and eye colour.

quick.overview:
Latanoprost is a prescription eye drop for glaucoma and raised eye pressure. Its label lists increased length, thickness and number of eyelashes, darker eyelid skin and darker iris pigmentation, so people interested in fuller lashes or deeper eye colour discuss it.

It is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue that increases fluid drainage from the eye; the lash and pigment changes come from the same drug class acting on lash follicles and pigment cells. Related analogues such as bimatoprost have been developed specifically for lash growth. No cosmetic trial of latanoprost has been published; a Phase 1/2 trial pairing it with laser in alopecia areata is registered.
quick.how: It is used as a prescribed eye drop in glaucoma care, with lash changes appearing as a side effect over weeks of regular use. Appearance communities mostly discuss it for eye darkening and lash growth as a curiosity.
quick.risks: Label warnings include permanent iris pigmentation change, eyelid darkening, inflammation and macular oedema, and a case report describes skin depigmentation. Iris darkening is listed as likely permanent. It is prescription-only and not approved for cosmetic use.

angle.text: Latanoprost, a glaucoma drop, lengthens and thickens lashes and can darken the iris as labelled side effects, giving fuller-looking eyes. These effects are documented from medical use; cosmetic trials have not been run.

onion-juice.summary: A folk scalp remedy pressed from onion bulbs and applied to regrow and thicken hair; one small alopecia areata trial reported more regrowth than water.

quick.overview:
Onion juice is pressed from onion bulbs and applied to the scalp as a natural way to regrow hair and thicken thinning areas. It circulates in social-media hair advice alongside rosemary oil and rice water.

The idea is that it stimulates follicles, with antioxidant effects and improved circulation proposed as general explanations. A small 2002 controlled trial in patchy alopecia areata reported more regrowth with onion juice than with tap water, and reviews describe the wider literature as small samples, mostly combination products.
quick.how: People apply the juice to the scalp, often as a mask or in a leave-in, a few times a week and leave it on before washing. Results are judged over months, and it is often combined with other natural or conventional hair treatments.
quick.risks: The sources report no specific safety data for scalp use. It is an unregulated food-derived preparation, and strong smell and skin irritation are common complaints. Reviews call for further study.

angle.text: Onion juice is applied to the scalp in the hope of stimulating follicles for regrowth and denser hair, often alongside rosemary oil. One small 2002 trial in alopecia areata reported more regrowth than water; trials in pattern baldness have not been done.

rosemary-oil.summary: A natural, minoxidil-style scalp and brow oil: a 2015 trial of 100 people found hair counts rose similarly to 2% minoxidil after six months.

quick.overview:
Rosemary oil is a plant essential oil applied to the scalp, and sometimes to brows and lashes, for thicker hair. It is popular as a natural alternative to minoxidil.

It is thought to work through improved microcirculation around follicles, and some forum users suggest effects on gene expression. A 2015 randomised trial of 100 people with androgenetic alopecia found hair counts rose in both rosemary oil and 2% minoxidil groups after six months, with no significant difference between them. Reviews describe the studies as few and small, and a 2025 Canadian consensus of eleven physicians did not recommend it.
quick.how: People dilute the oil in a carrier oil or use it in shampoos and scalp serums, massaging it in several times a week. Results are judged over about six months, and it is often used alongside other hair treatments.
quick.risks: Reviews describe a minimal side-effect profile, and the 2015 trial reported scalp itching less often than with minoxidil. Undiluted essential oil can irritate skin. It is sold as a cosmetic or aromatherapy product rather than an approved hair-loss drug.

angle.text: Rosemary oil is used as a natural alternative to minoxidil, applied to scalp, brows or lashes for thicker growth through improved microcirculation around follicles. A 2015 trial of 100 people compared it with 2% minoxidil for pattern hair loss; brow and lash uses are anecdotal.

anastrozole.summary: A breast-cancer aromatase inhibitor that teen heightmaxxers discuss for keeping growth plates open and TRT users for oestrogen control; no trials show a height gain in healthy people.

quick.overview:
Anastrozole is a prescription aromatase inhibitor approved for breast cancer in postmenopausal women. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed for delaying growth-plate closure to add adult height, and by TRT users for keeping oestrogen low.

It blocks aromatase, the enzyme that converts testosterone and androstenedione to oestrogen, lowering oestradiol. Oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, which is the basis of the height interest. No controlled trial shows a height gain in healthy adolescents, and a 2023 gynecomastia review says it has not been consistently useful in boys.
quick.how: Heightmaxxers discuss it alongside growth hormone and similar compounds, while TRT users discuss it as part of oestrogen management. It is prescription-only, and height use is off-label.
quick.risks: The label lists reduced bone density, higher cholesterol, cardiovascular events in women with heart disease and fetal harm. Forum users report fatigue and crashed oestrogen. Use for height in adolescents is off-label and untested.

angle.text: Anastrozole lowers oestrogen, and since oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, teen heightmaxxers hope it keeps plates open for extra adult height; TRT users use it for oestrogen control. Its approved use is breast cancer, and the height idea has not been tested in healthy people.

letrozole.summary: A potent aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer and fertility that heightmaxxers consider for delaying growth plates; no trials in healthy teens exist.

quick.overview:
Letrozole is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal breast cancer and is also widely used in fertility treatment. Looksmax.org users, including teenagers, discuss it for delaying growth-plate closure to add height, and some link lower oestrogen to leanness.

It blocks the aromatase enzyme, lowering conversion of androgens to oestrogen. Since oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, the hope is a longer growth window. No controlled trial in healthy adolescents testing it for adult height was found, and forum users describe it as the most potent option and the most likely to crash oestrogen.
quick.how: Heightmaxxers discuss it alongside growth hormone or MK-677 and compare it with anastrozole and exemestane. It is prescription-only, and height use is off-label.
quick.risks: The label lists bone density loss, raised cholesterol, fatigue and dizziness, hot flashes and joint pain, and it can cause fetal harm and is contraindicated in pregnancy. Height use is off-label and untested in adolescents.

angle.text: Letrozole lowers oestrogen strongly, and heightmaxxers hope this delays growth-plate closure for extra adult height; some users also link low oestrogen to leanness. Trials cover breast cancer and fertility, not height in healthy people.

exemestane.summary: A steroidal breast-cancer aromatase inhibitor that teen heightmaxxers favour as the milder option for keeping growth plates open; no trials in healthy adolescents.

quick.overview:
Exemestane is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal breast cancer. On looksmax.org, mostly teenagers discuss it as a way to keep growth plates open for extra height, often alongside growth hormone.

It irreversibly inactivates aromatase and is a steroid structurally related to androstenedione, lowering oestrogen, which is thought to delay growth-plate fusion. Some users call it milder than anastrozole or letrozole and note androgenic properties. No trial has tested it for height or appearance in healthy adolescents.
quick.how: It is discussed as an alternative to the other aromatase inhibitors, usually combined with growth-hormone approaches in heightmaxxing threads. It is prescription-only, and height use is off-label.
quick.risks: The label lists bone density loss over time, hot flushes, fatigue, joint pain and fetal harm, and a maculopathy case report exists. Forum users report hair and hormone problems. Height use is off-label and untested.

angle.text: Exemestane inactivates aromatase to lower oestrogen, which teen heightmaxxers hope keeps growth plates open for extra height; it is favoured as the milder option. It is approved for breast cancer, and the height use rests on forum reports.

tamoxifen.summary: A breast-cancer oestrogen-receptor blocker that bodybuilders and TRT users take to treat or prevent gynecomastia for a leaner, more defined chest.

quick.overview:
Tamoxifen is a prescription oestrogen-receptor blocker for breast cancer. In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles it is used off-label to treat or prevent gynecomastia and to manage oestrogen during steroid or TRT use, for a leaner, more defined chest.

It binds oestrogen receptors, blocking oestrogen's effect in breast tissue while acting like oestrogen in tissues such as bone and endometrium. A review says it has been tried successfully in adolescent gynecomastia; no trials address its other cosmetic uses, and some users ask about growth-plate effects with conflicting lab findings.
quick.how: Users take it during or after steroid and TRT use, often as part of post-cycle routines, or when breast tissue appears. It is prescription-only, and appearance uses are off-label.
quick.risks: The US label carries a boxed warning for uterine cancers, stroke and pulmonary embolism in the oncology setting, and lists liver effects, hot flashes and fetal harm. Retinopathy and low platelets have been reported.

angle.text: Tamoxifen blocks oestrogen in breast tissue, which is why bodybuilders and TRT users take it to treat or prevent gynecomastia and keep the chest lean and defined. It has been studied for male gynecomastia; muscle-gain claims are anecdotal.

clomiphene.summary: A fertility drug that men use off-label to lift their own testosterone without injections, for more muscle and leanness; studied in hypogonadal men, not for looks.

quick.overview:
Clomiphene is a prescription drug for ovulation induction in women. Men use it off-label to raise their own testosterone and recover after steroid cycles, and looksmax.org discusses it under 'tmaxxing' in pursuit of muscle, leanness and energy.

It blocks oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary, raising gonadotropins and prompting the testes to make more testosterone. A 2022 systematic review covered 19 studies, four randomised, of clomiphene in men with hypogonadism; no trials test it for cosmetic goals in healthy people.
quick.how: Men take it as a tablet through a prescriber for low testosterone, or as part of post-cycle routines in physique communities. Hormone changes build over weeks and are tracked with blood tests.
quick.risks: The label lists ovarian enlargement and flushes, plus visual disturbances that may be irreversible. Users report mood and libido changes. It is prescription-only and male use is off-label.

angle.text: Clomiphene blocks oestrogen feedback in the brain so the body raises its own testosterone, which men use in pursuit of muscle, leanness and energy without injections. It has been studied in hypogonadal men; effects on looks are untested.

enclomiphene.summary: The trans-isomer of clomiphene, studied for raising testosterone in men with secondary hypogonadism while preserving fertility; forum appearance and height use is untested.

quick.overview:
Enclomiphene is one of the two isomers that make up clomiphene citrate. It was developed as an oral treatment for men with low testosterone from reduced pituitary signalling, and appearance communities discuss it as a way to raise testosterone without injecting it, for muscle, leanness and energy.

It blocks oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary, raising LH and FSH so the testes make more testosterone, while preserving sperm counts in trials against topical testosterone. A 2025 meta-analysis of randomised trials of clomiphene or enclomiphene reported higher total testosterone, LH and FSH than placebo, with considerable heterogeneity. Some posters link it to height or bone growth, which no trial has tested.
quick.how: Men use it as an oral alternative to testosterone injections, as part of post-cycle or TRT-adjacent routines, with hormone levels tracked by blood tests. Changes appear over weeks.
quick.risks: Published trials describe short-term safety comparable to placebo and testosterone gel, but long-term data are limited. Forum users report fatigue and mood effects. It has no FDA approval, products outside prescriptions are of uncertain quality, and teen data are absent.

angle.text: Enclomiphene blocks oestrogen feedback in the brain so the body makes more of its own testosterone, with fertility and testicle size preserved, which men use for muscle, leanness and energy. Trials were in men with secondary hypogonadism; appearance and height uses are untested.

nicotine.summary: The stimulant in tobacco, pouches, gum and vapes, used by some in appearance communities to blunt appetite and stay lean; highly addictive, and no trials test it for leanness.

quick.overview:
Nicotine is the main psychoactive alkaloid in tobacco, sold in cigarettes, vapes, oral pouches, gum, lozenges and patches. In looksmaxxing forums it is used to suppress appetite for a leaner look and as a focus aid, while other posters argue it harms skin, teeth, hair and sleep.

It activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, prompting release of dopamine and other neurotransmitters; forum posts attribute lower appetite and higher energy expenditure to this action. The cessation literature is large, but no clinical study has tested nicotine as a fat-loss or appearance intervention.
quick.how: People use pouches, gum or vapes for a stimulant lift between meals or during cuts. Regulated nicotine replacement products are labelled for easing withdrawal in people quitting smoking, not for weight loss.
quick.risks: Nicotine is highly addictive and raises heart rate and blood pressure; gum labels caution people with heart disease and pregnant users. Forum users report insomnia, anxiety, palpitations and dependence, and long-term data on pouches and vapes are still accumulating.

angle.text: Nicotine is used as a stimulant appetite suppressant: less hunger means fewer calories and a leaner look, and it doubles as a focus aid. Trials have not tested it for leanness, and forum posters debate effects on skin, hair and teeth.

benzoyl-peroxide.summary: The over-the-counter acne staple that kills acne bacteria and unclogs pores for clearer skin; backed by guidelines and decades of trials, with dryness and irritation as the trade-off.

quick.overview:
Benzoyl peroxide is a topical antibacterial and peeling agent sold in washes, creams and gels, mostly for acne, and is also found in prescription combinations with adapalene or clindamycin. People use it for fewer breakouts and clearer skin, and some also use the wash on the body for breakouts and odor.

It releases oxygen radicals that act against Cutibacterium acnes and has a keratolytic effect that helps unclog pores. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline gives it a strong recommendation, and a 2022 network meta-analysis found a combined retinoid and benzoyl peroxide the most effective topical option among those assessed for mild-to-moderate acne. The odor use is anecdotal.
quick.how: It is used as a wash or leave-on gel, often once or twice a day, and is commonly paired with a topical retinoid. Improvement typically builds over several weeks, and many users use it during testosterone or steroid use.
quick.risks: Dryness, peeling, redness and stinging are the most common effects, and irritation is more likely when another topical acne medicine is used at the same time. It bleaches fabric and hair. Animal studies from 1981 reported tumour-promoting activity in mice; clinical relevance is not established.

angle.text: Benzoyl peroxide kills acne bacteria and exfoliates, giving fewer breakouts and clearer skin. Its acne use is backed by guidelines and decades of trials; using the wash on the body for odor is anecdotal.

snail-mucin.summary: The Korean-skincare staple made from snail secretion, used for hydration, a glowing look, fading acne marks and softer fine lines; small studies so far.

quick.overview:
Snail mucin, or snail secretion filtrate, is the mucus of snails used in serums, essences and creams, especially in Korean skincare. People use it for hydrated, glowing skin, fading acne marks and softening fine lines.

It contains allantoin, glycolic acid, hyaluronic acid-type glycosaminoglycans, proteins and peptides, which may support hydration and surface smoothness, and cell and animal studies link its peptides with antimicrobial, antioxidant and wound-healing effects. Reviews describe uses in hydration, anti-aging, acne, scarring and hyperpigmentation, based on mostly preclinical or small studies, and a 2022 randomised trial examined a serum with it in mask-related acne.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum, essence or cream after cleansing, usually daily, and layered under moisturiser and sunscreen. Hydration is felt quickly, while marks and texture change over weeks.
quick.risks: Reviews flag skin irritation, sensitisation and allergic reactions as possible, and note that standardised formulations and formal toxicology monographs are lacking. Labels advise external use only and avoiding the eyes.

angle.text: Snail mucin supplies humectants and repair compounds that improve hydration and smooth texture, leaving skin plumper and more even, and helping acne marks fade. Reviews describe small studies on hydration and scars, with large trials still to come.

centella-asiatica.summary: Gotu kola, the 'cica' plant in many calming Korean skincare products, used to reduce redness and help marks and scars heal; trials exist for wound and scar healing.

quick.overview:
Centella asiatica, or cica, is a creeping plant long used in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine and now common in calming skincare. People use it to reduce redness, help acne marks and scars heal, and support smoother, clearer skin.

In cell and animal studies, its triterpenes (asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid) stimulate collagen I and growth factors involved in repair and reduce inflammatory markers such as IL-1 beta and IL-6. A 2022 systematic review of four clinical trials concluded it might enhance wound healing, and small trials cover aging skin and post-procedure recovery.
quick.how: It is applied as a cream, serum or mask, often after treatments or during irritation flares, and used daily. Calming is noticeable early, while scar and texture changes build over weeks.
quick.risks: The sources give little safety detail; topical and oral products carry the usual precautions. Oral use appears in trials in diabetes and cognition, which sit outside appearance use. Reviews recommend further research on safety, dosing and standardisation.

angle.text: Centella asiatica's triterpenes calm and repair skin, giving less redness, faster healing of marks and scars, and smoother skin. Trials exist for wound and scar healing; evidence for anti-aging is small and mixed in quality.

bakuchiol.summary: A plant-derived 'retinol alternative' for wrinkles, pigmentation and acne, favoured by people who find retinol irritating; small trials report retinol-like results.

quick.overview:
Bakuchiol is a phenolic compound extracted mainly from the seeds of Psoralea corylifolia and marketed as a gentler alternative to retinol in creams and serums. People use it for fewer visible wrinkles, more even pigmentation and clearer skin.

Although it is structurally unrelated to retinoids, a 2014 study reported it regulates many of the same genes as retinol, supporting collagen and epidermal renewal without acting through retinoid receptors. A 2019 randomised trial compared it with retinol for facial photoageing, and a 2022 systematic review of 30 articles (seven clinical) found results comparable to retinoids in photoaging, acne and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
quick.how: It is applied as a daily serum or moisturiser, morning or night, often by people who cannot tolerate retinol. Texture and pigment changes build over several months.
quick.risks: Reviews say it lacks the burning and scaling common with topical retinoids, though one systematic review notes an adverse event report. Labels advise avoiding the eyes and broken skin and stopping if irritation occurs. It shows estrogen-receptor activity in lab studies, whose clinical meaning in skin products is not established.

angle.text: Bakuchiol sends retinol-like signals in skin, smoothing texture and reducing pigmentation and visible wrinkles with less irritation. A handful of small trials report retinol-like results.

mandelic-acid.summary: A larger, slower-penetrating alpha-hydroxy acid used in gentle peels and serums to clear pores and fade dark spots, popular with sensitive skin.

quick.overview:
Mandelic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid used as a chemical exfoliant for acne, dark spots, uneven pigmentation and photoaging. It is sold in serums and professional peels and favoured by people with sensitive skin.

Its molecule is larger than glycolic acid's, which is said to slow penetration and reduce irritation, and as an AHA it promotes exfoliation and cell turnover, leaving fewer clogged pores and smoother, more even skin. A Cochrane review covered AHAs for acne as a class, and registered trials compare mandelic peels with tranexamic acid for melasma and test a combined peel around the eyes.
quick.how: It is used as a leave-on serum a few evenings a week or as a professional peel, and often built up slowly. Sunscreen is generally advised with AHA products, and results show over weeks.
quick.risks: Common AHA effects are stinging, redness and peeling, and sun sensitivity is a consideration. The sources give little mandelic-acid-specific safety data.

angle.text: Mandelic acid gently exfoliates dead cells, so pores clog less and dark spots fade for smoother, more even skin. Dedicated clinical evidence is limited, with most support coming from related AHAs.

tea-tree-oil.summary: An Australian essential oil used on skin and scalp for fewer breakouts, less odor and cleaner-feeling skin, with small acne and eyelid-mite trials.

quick.overview:
Tea tree oil is the essential oil distilled from Melaleuca alternifolia leaves, used in soaps, washes, gels and shampoos for acne, post-shave breakouts, body odor, scalp care and eyelid cleansing, aiming at clearer skin and a healthier scalp.

Its main component, terpinen-4-ol, disrupts bacterial and yeast membranes in lab studies and suppresses inflammatory mediators in human monocytes. Human evidence includes small pilot trials, such as a 5% acne gel pilot with 18 people, and eyelid-mite studies. Claims of lowering testosterone and helping shaving rest on anecdote.
quick.how: It is used diluted, as a spot treatment, in a wash or shampoo or a premixed gel, applied topically. Skin changes show over weeks of regular use.
quick.risks: Irritation and allergic contact dermatitis are documented, with reactions in a small percentage of users, and swallowing is toxic. Labels advise external use only, and pure oil is generally diluted.

angle.text: Tea tree oil's antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory action means fewer breakouts and less odor, for clearer skin and a healthier scalp. Small trials exist for acne and eyelid mites; the testosterone and shaving claims are anecdotal.

squalane.summary: A lightweight, shelf-stable moisturising oil that leaves skin soft, hydrated and smooth right away; used in serums, moisturisers, lips and hair.

quick.overview:
Squalane is a stable oil made by hydrogenating squalene, a lipid also found in human skin oil. It is used in serums, facial oils, moisturisers, lip products and hair products to leave skin soft and supple, with a non-greasy feel suited to many skin types.

As an emollient and occlusive lipid it helps the skin hold water, so the smoother, hydrated look appears immediately. Reviews report hydrating and emollient activity mainly from animal and laboratory work, and few controlled trials have tested squalane on its own; one small trial of a fullerene-in-squalane product did not isolate its effect.
quick.how: It is applied daily as a few drops or a cream, usually as a final step over serums to seal moisture, and also used on lips and hair ends. The feel is immediate, and barrier changes build over weeks.
quick.risks: Sources describe low irritation potential and generally suggest patch testing for sensitive skin. It is sold over the counter as a cosmetic ingredient, and may be plant-derived or historically shark-derived.

angle.text: Squalane is a lightweight oil that seals moisture into skin, so it feels softer and looks smoother and more hydrated right after application. Trial data specific to squalane is limited.
